I think direct index is more consistent with the old behavior and more consistent with other find functions, including with other similar languages like Python. We discussed this recently in a core meeting. It was decided not to expose the `find_sequence` functions at this time, because the demand is unclear. It is preferable to make a GDextension with `find_sequence` as a feature.
The refactors are welcome, however, so the PR just needs to be downsized a bit.

Busy few months for me, but I had time tonight and wrote a Find_Sequence GDExtension in C++. It performs much worse than a native Find_Sequence implementation, and I would like to return to my proposal of adding this function natively to the engine. Methodology: I rebased this PR onto master, syncing it to the most recent builds of 4.5. I added a Find_Sequence to Core/Templates/Vector.h, and exposed it to PackedByteArray in Core/Variant/Variant_call.cpp. The GDExtension was written in C++, and implements the same search algorithm, taking two PackedByteArrays as input. 100 trials searching 134.2 MB file (retrieved via FileAccess.get_file_as_bytes()) for a Byte Sequence occurring early in the file. I tested 1. A GDScript implementation of the algorithm 2. Using the Native String.find() on a Hexadecimal String of the file (which calls the backend Span.find_sequence) 3. Using a Native PackedByteArray.find_sequence (implemented to directly call backend Span.find_sequence) 4. Using the C++ GDExtension find_sequence Results: 1. GDScript Find Sequence elapsed 8.1967830657959 2. String Find Sequence elapsed 1.37343001365662 3. Native Find Sequence elapsed 0.26774501800537 4. GDExtension Find Sequence elapsed 4.45171809196472 I've attached some screenshots of the relevant code, I believe I wrote each behavior as optimally as I could.

I've already responded on another platform, but for completeness' sake I'll respond here as well.

A GDExtension implementation is expected to be (almost) exactly as fast as a potential native Godot implementation. That was the reason we recommended to expose this functionality in GDExtension instead of natively in `Array` and `Packed*Array`.

The reason your current implementation is slow is because you're using `Packed*Array` indexing. Indexing into `Packed*Array` makes a call through the GDExtension API, which is slow in multiple respects. In order to achieve the same speed as a native implementation, you should query the data pointer (`p_search.ptr()`) and size from `p_search` and search through the pointer instead of through the `Packed*Array`. 

_(note that this discussion doesn't pertain to the PR at hand, which is so far unchanged from the version I approved)_

```

Hi! I'm happy to clear up the decision we made.

> My understanding was the languages are supposed to be similar.

GDScript shares some similarities to Python, but we need to make decisions that are the right fit for Godot. In this case, we could not make the same decision as Python.
You may be aware of this already, but I'd just like to clarify that a result of `-1` indicates that the string could not be found, not that it was found in the last position. This becomes more obvious with a longer example:

```python
"ABCDEFG".find("CD", -1)
>>> -1
```

The old Godot implementation would return `2` in this scenario, since it would (depending on the function...) interpret negative indices as "just ignore the index, search from the start". Since `-1` is the default index passed to some functions (e.g. `rfind`), we cannot break this behavior. Passing in `-1` must return a valid result.

That left us with [several other choices](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/104332#issuecomment-2738829234). @ColinSORourke suggested interpreting negative indexes as "indexes from the back of the search string", same as python. However, different from Python, he suggested being lenient with small negative numbers, and rounding down to the first valid search index, to account for possible `-1` values being passed. This would result in this behavior:

```gdscript
"AAABAAA".rfind("AA", -1) # start search at the last character (rounded down to the second-to-last character)
# Returns 5

"AAABAAA".rfind("AA", -2) # start search at the second-to-last character
# Returns 5

"AAABAAA".rfind("AA", -3) # start search from the third-to-last character
# Returns 4
```

My suggestion was to do the same as we do from the front, just with negative indices. That means that `-1` searches from the last possible position (similar to `0` from the front), `-2` excludes the last character from being searched (similar to `1` from the front), etc. This becomes useful in case you want to exclude some characters from the back of the search:

```gdscript
"AAABAAA".rfind("AA", -1) # search from the very back
# Returns 5

"AAABAAA".rfind("AA", -2) # skip the last A
# Returns 4

"AAABAAA".rfind("AA", -3) # skip the last two A
# Returns 1
```

This is of course the same as if the search was reversed:

```gdscript
"AAABAAA".find("AA", 0) # search from the very front
# Returns 0

"AAABAAA".find("AA", 1) # skip the first A
# Returns 1

"AAABAAA".find("AA", 2) # skip the first two A
# Returns 4
```

From my point of view, this is the correct abstraction over negative indices, because it treats negative indices the same as it treats positive indices, just from the back of the string. However, @ColinSORourke's approach is arguably easier to understand. 
Since most people won't use negative indices that aren't `-1`, it's probably not super important which of the two we choose. I felt more comfortable going with an internally consistent abstraction than one that might be easier to understand, but needs extra rules to work in the way we need it, so we merged my suggestion in the end.

https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.rfind

> str.rfind(sub[, start[, end]])
> 
> Return the highest index in the string where substring sub is found, such that sub is contained within s[start:end]. Optional arguments start and end are interpreted as in slice notation. Return -1 on failure.

> The idea of skipping the last characters is nice, but I am having a hard time understanding the "start from" part.
> Do you mean when the index is negative find behaves like rfind and vice-versa?

`find` performs forward search no matter the index given, and `rfind` performs a backwards search. Negative indexes are converted to positive indexes before starting the search. They do not have any effect on the search direction.

> I still do not understand why it says "Search C->D" here (instead of A->E)
> 
> ```gdscript
> "ABCDEF".find("BCD", -2)
> // Old behavior: Don't search, return -1
> // New Behavior: Search C->D, return -1
> ```

`find` performs a forward search. With `from=-1`, it would start with `"DEF" == "BCD"`, because that's the last possible position to search. With `-2`, it will instead start at `"CDE" == "BCD"`, because that's the second-to-last possible position. It will then proceed to the next position (the `"DEF"` one). So you could say it searches `C->D`.

> I might be misunderstanding this. In Python's there's an optional third parameter to specify the `end` (if you want to skip the last n characters).

This might be interesting for us as well, but hasn't been implemented. `find` will always search to the end of the string, while `rfind` always searches to the start of the string. With a second parameter, this could be limited. But it doesn't have to do with negative indexes.

If you're familiar with git, our [Pull request workflow](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/organization/pull_requests/creating_pull_requests.html) should be very familiar with you: Fork Godot, make your edits, and open a pull request.

The docs in question are located in the file `doc/classes/String.xml`.
We have an [explainer article](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/engine_details/class_reference/index.html) and [contribution guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/documentation/class_reference.html) about the docs xml file format. But to give you a shortcut, you just need to find the `<method name="find" qualifiers="const">` entry and edit its `<description>` accordingly.

Let me know if that works for you! I'm happy to give assistance if you need any.
